title: Context wrangling notelets — quick hits and experiment log
text:
TL;DR:
Quick scratchpad about strategies for reducing tail latency and cost when handling >16k token sessions. Not a formal doc — mostly heuristics, a few small benchmarks, and next-step experiments.

Motivation / problem framing:
- Customers are increasingly pushing very long contexts (documents + multi-turn history). We need cheap ways to preserve salient context without blowing up token cost or latency.
- Tradeoffs: keep fidelity (avoid hallucination/regression) vs speed/cost. Operational constraints: autoscaling, memory fragmentation on multi-tenant machines, kv-cache eviction behavior.

Quick concept summaries (one-liners I want to remember):
- Chunk-anchor + priority eviction: tag chunks with extractive salience score at ingestion, keep high-salience chunks in KV; evict low-salience first. Cheap salience: lexical overlap with last user message + BM25-ish sketch.
- Rolling prefix snapshot (delta-apply): periodically materialize compressed KV snapshots to avoid rehydrating full context for warm starts. Snapshots stored per-session with small diffs.
- Hybrid sparse/dense: use sparse local attention for full window + dense attention on anchored regions (queries + recent n tokens).

Papers / reads (short notes):
- Longformer (arXiv:2004.05150): sliding-window attention + global tokens. Takeaway: sliding windows are robust but need tuning for chunk boundary effects (off-by-one hallucinations when answer straddles chunk). For us: consider dynamic global tokens (derived from salience).
- Prefix-cache / Latency papers (various infra blog posts): key idea is amortizing KV store rehydration cost across sessions. Implementation nuance: snapshot size vs restore time is non-linear because of allocator + CUDA memcpy overhead.
- Perceiver/latent approaches (review notes): compress long input into fixed-size latent then attend. Promising but hard to integrate with retrieval workflows where passages must remain intact for grounding.

Mini-experiment log (local dev VM on p4d-ish infra, very rough):
- Setup: 8x768-d model variant (toy), sequence sliced into 4k windows with 1k overlap, backend with continuous KV caching enabled.
- Baseline: full re-feed each request (no KV) = median 220ms for 512 token generation, p95 ~ 480ms.
- KV enabled, naive eviction (LRU): median 180ms, p95 ~ 420ms.
- KV + salience-prioritized eviction (cheap lexical score): median 170ms, p95 ~ 350ms. Observations: p95 improvement mostly from avoiding rehydration of very large KVs in 20% of tests that had many long documents.
- Snapshot experiment: storing small binary snapshots (zstd level 3) reduced restore time by ~40% for large KVs vs re-compute; but snapshot creation added ~12ms per write which may matter at high QPS.

Micro-bench notes (numbers are noisy):
- memcpy (host->device) for 64MB chunk: ~8-12ms depending on bus; CUDA allocator fragmentation can add 10-50ms tail if many allocs.
- zstd compression for KV -> snapshot (64MB) on vCPU single-thread: 200ms compress, 25ms decompress — suggests snapshot-on-write expensive, snapshot-on-read cheaper but delays first restore.

Heuristics that seem promising to try next (prioritized):
1) Salience-tiered KV with two buckets: hot (keep in GPU), warm (compressed on host + fast decompress), cold (evict). Fast path check: if token in hot -> serve from KV; warm -> decompress async and serve incremental.
2) Delta snapshots: write small diffs every N updates (N chosen by QPS) and full snapshot less often. Full snapshot creation scheduled during low load windows.
3) Chunk-coalescing at ingestion: merge small passages into ~4–8KB logical chunks to reduce metadata overhead and reduce fragmentation.
4) Backoff policy for global attention: if budget exceeded, switch to anchored-global tokens computed by a cheap BM25 pass.

Operational notes / constraints:
- Need to watch GPU memory pressure: pinned pages for KV lead to higher swap risk under noisy neighbor workloads. Consider per-customer memory caps or soft-fails with fallback to smaller quantized model.
- Tracing: instrument a fine-grained metric 'kv-restore-latency' (histogram) and 'snapshot-create-duration' to correlate with p95 gen latency spikes.

Open questions / things to validate:
- How often do chunk boundaries actually cause hallucination regressions in our eval prompts? (Need an automated regression test: take eval prompts, shift chunk boundaries random +/- 128 tokens and check fidelity.)
- Is warm-host decompress + async streaming workable at 100rps? Need load test with realistic latency target.
- Cost calc: what's break-even for storing hot KV in GPU vs recompute? Build a simple cost model: GPU mem cost per GB-hour vs CPU+IO cost for rehydration and added latency penalty (SLA hit cost).

Short todo list (for next 2 weeks):
- [ ] Implement cheap BM25-ish salience scorer prototype (python) and run across 2k archived sessions to get distribution of scores (owner: Luca).
- [ ] Add kv-restore-latency histogram to runtime tracing (owner: Mina).
- [ ] Prototype warm-host compressed snapshot flow in runtime branch (PR: linked above) and run perf test (owner: Hannah / Luca).
- [ ] Create regression harness for chunk-boundary hallucination test and run on eval set (owner: research).

Notes to self: keep writeups short — stakeholders want decisions + numbers. If an approach reduces p95 by >20% with <10% CPU overhead, it's probably worth shipping as opt-in.

References / reading backlog (to triage later):
- Longformer (sliding-window attention) — arXiv link in linked_artifacts
- Blog: "KV snapshotting patterns" (internal) — check slack thread #kv-ops
- Perf PR: runtime/pull/482 (prototype warm snapshot flow)

Random brainstorming (low-fidelity):
- Use a lightweight transformer (T0-ish distill) to compute salience per chunk cheaply on host, then use that signal for both eviction and for constructing anchored global tokens.
- Explore a dual-store retrieval: dense for semantics (to pick anchors) + lexical to preserve exact spans for quoting.

End of notelets. Will revisit after Mina's trace metrics land.
